name: Bilal Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a sports reporter for the regional evening paper and its website. I cover the city's football club, which plays in the second tier, plus the non-league clubs around it. A normal day is the training ground at ten for the manager's press conference, then back to write it up, then phoning the smaller clubs for team news. Saturdays and Tuesday nights I'm at matches, filing a report on the final whistle.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love match days, the noise, the press box, the pie at half-time. What wears me out is filing fast on the whistle, I'm still too slow, and Steve, the sports editor, ends up tidying my intro. I also don't use any of those AI tools. I've seen what they write about football and it reads like a betting website.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's more or less what I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, in the pub with the lads from the other papers. Football's about people and atmosphere, and AI was never going to sit in a freezing press box. I wouldn't post about it, I don't really do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be a bit worried, but not about AI. The paper cut the print edition to three days a week last year and the sports desk went from four to three. I've stood in the rain at a fifth-tier ground on a Tuesday night with six other people, and no software is doing that for me. The question is whether anyone keeps paying me to be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my head down and get faster on the whistle. I'd keep saving like I do, about five hundred a month, because Hana and I are getting married next summer. And I'd keep my contacts at the club warm, the press officer especially, because that's how you hear about jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but nothing new. It's the same worry everyone in local papers has had for ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of a cushion do you have going into the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About eight months of pay saved, because I lived with my parents till 25 and didn't spend much. My car's paid off. The wedding will take a chunk, but we've kept it modest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the paper cut another sports post, would it be you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah, I'm the newest. But there's a sports website and two radio stations in the city that use freelancers. I'd find something, I just wouldn't love it.

say: I'd say **football is people** and atmosphere, and AI was never going to sit in a press box.
I'd say **told you so** in the pub, not online.
think: Privately I'm still worried, because the paper cut the **print edition** to three days.
The **sports desk** went from four to three, and I'm the newest.
do: Get **faster on the whistle** when filing match reports.
Keep saving about **five hundred** a month before the wedding.
Keep the **club press officer** on side for job tips.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, the same worry local papers have carried for **ten years**.
S0.quote: I've stood in the rain at a fifth-tier ground on a Tuesday night with six other people, and no software is doing that for me.
fieldNote: His worry here is the **paper's decline**, not AI.
He's the **newest on the desk**, which he states plainly.
He keeps his opinions **offline**, preferring the pub to posts.

steps.text: Practise filing match reports faster on the final whistle
Save five hundred a month ahead of the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I don't like. Writing and checking is the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say papers need to be careful, because readers can tell when nobody was at the game. I'd say it to Steve, and to the lads at other papers. I'm not going to start a campaign, but I'd make the point when it came up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A match report is mostly the score, the scorers and a few lines from the manager, and a computer could do that before the players reach the tunnel. That's the honest truth. The non-league round-ups would go first, and that's half my week. I think the desk would go from three to two, and I'd be the one out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still not use the tools, I'd rather be known as the one who's actually at the ground. I'd cut the wedding back a bit, fewer guests, and keep more cash. I'd ask the club press officer outright whether they'd be hiring for match-day media. And I'd keep an eye on the jobs board every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. I've only been doing this four years and it's what I always wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't use the tools. Even if that cost you the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'm being stubborn. I just don't trust them, and I've never needed them. If Steve told me to, I'd do it, but I wouldn't volunteer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Hana say about cutting the wedding back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be fine, honestly she's more sensible than me. She's a pharmacist, steady job. It's my mum who'd be upset about the guest list.

say: I'd say **readers can tell** when nobody from the paper was at the game.
I'd make the point to **my editor** and other reporters, not start a campaign.
think: Privately a **match report** is mostly score, scorers and quotes a computer could do.
I think the desk drops from three to two, and **I'd be out**.
do: Cut the **wedding guest list** to keep more cash.
Ask the **club press officer** about match-day media jobs.
feel: **Worried**, because this is the job he always wanted.
S1.quote: A match report is mostly the score, the scorers and a few lines from the manager, and a computer could do that before the players reach the tunnel.
fieldNote: He's **clear-eyed** about how routine his match reports are.
He'd still **refuse the tools** unless told to, a clear contradiction he half admits.
His **fiancée's steady job** softens the blow at home.

steps.text: Cut the wedding guest list to keep more cash
Ask the club press officer about match-day media jobs
Move wedding savings into a separate account he won't touch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's before the club's next stadium plans even get approved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and somebody should have seen it coming. I'd want the government to do something for people like me who are only starting out. I'm not a protest person, but I'd vote for whoever had a real plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the job's gone, simple as that. My work is all writing and phoning, so it goes in 2028. My fiancée is a pharmacist and I write about football, and in two years her job would be the one paying for our wedding. Hana's work has a hands-on side, so she gets a bit longer, though dispensing pills isn't exactly safe either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd go ahead with the wedding but make it small, family only. I'd keep all my savings in cash. I'd try hard for a job at the club, match-day stuff where you're physically there, filming, interviews in the tunnel. I'd wait before retraining, because I don't know what to retrain into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty awful. Like the final whistle going when you're two down and you haven't had a shot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad first, he drives a bus, so he'd understand. He'd say get something with your hands. He's said that since I was sixteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you listen to him this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yeah. But robots for hands-on work are only three years behind in this picture. So I don't know where that leaves anyone.

say: I'd say it's **madness** that nobody saw it coming.
I'd **vote** for whoever had a real plan for people starting out.
think: Privately my job is **gone in 2028**, because it's all writing and phoning.
My **fiancée's pharmacy job** would pay for the wedding, and hers isn't fully safe either.
do: Chase a **match-day job** at the club doing tunnel interviews and filming.
feel: **Awful**, like being two down at the final whistle without a shot.
S2.quote: My fiancée is a pharmacist and I write about football, and in two years her job would be the one paying for our wedding.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the job** and says so flatly.
He'd **wait** before retraining because he can't see a safe target.
His father's advice to **work with his hands** comes back, but robots blunt it.

steps.text: Hold a family-only wedding next summer
Keep all eight months of savings in cash
Apply for match-day media work at the city's football club
Hold off on choosing any retraining course for now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's like a full contract for a player.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this sensibly, but people need to start now. I'd say the government and the papers should both help with training. I'd mention it on the podcast I do with a mate, but not make a big thing of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd try to get inside the club itself, because somebody still has to stand next to the manager on a match day. The writing goes in 2031, but the being-there part lasts a bit longer, maybe to 2034. And clubs like having their own people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the paper for now and keep getting better. I'd get the club press officer to put me forward for any media role, even part-time. We'd have the wedding as planned. And I'd put a bit more each month into savings, maybe seven hundred instead of five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd feel like I could do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, by year two or three, if the club wanted it. I'd be one of the last, though. My mate on the podcast already uses them and he gives me grief about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the podcast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just me and my mate Kev, who works at a bank, talking about the club every Monday. About four hundred listeners. It's a hobby, but it's the one thing I do that's really mine.

say: I'd say there's **time to be sensible**, but people must start now.
I'd ask the **government and papers** to help with training.
think: Privately I'd try to get **inside the club**, where someone still stands by the manager.
The writing goes in 2031, but **being there** lasts until about 2034.
do: Ask the press officer to put him forward for a **club media role**.
Raise savings to **seven hundred** a month.
Go ahead with the **wedding** as planned.
feel: **Worried**, but feeling there's something he can do.
S3.quote: With five years I'd try to get inside the club itself, because somebody still has to stand next to the manager on a match day.
fieldNote: He spots the **hands-on gap** between AGI and robots and aims for it.
He'd learn the tools only if **the club** wanted it.
His **podcast** is a small passion that could grow, though he doesn't see it that way yet.

steps.text: Ask the club press officer to recommend him for media roles
Raise monthly savings from five hundred to seven hundred
Stay at the paper and keep covering the second-tier club

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long way off. I'd be 37.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so nobody should panic. I'd say that to the lads at work too, because some of them get worked up about every headline. Plan, don't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough that I'd probably just keep my head down and enjoy the football, which I know is exactly what I shouldn't do. I know AGI comes for the writing in 2036. But in the next few years my job looks about the same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at the paper, get married, maybe buy a house with Hana in a couple of years. I'd keep saving. Around 2030 I'd start properly looking at club jobs or something in coaching, since I did my coaching badges at uni.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It's something to think about later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your head down. What would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the paper started using AI for the non-league stuff. That'd be my warning sign. Or if Steve left, because he protects me a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the coaching badges.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I did the basic coaching level at uni and coached an under-twelves team for two years. I loved it, honestly. Standing on a pitch with kids is about as far from a robot's job as I can think of.

say: I'd say there's time, so **plan, don't panic**.
I'd tell colleagues at the paper to **stop reacting** to every scary headline about AI.
think: Privately I'd probably **keep my head down**, which I know is wrong.
My job looks **about the same** for the next few years.
do: Get married and maybe **buy a house** with Hana in two years.
Look at **club jobs or coaching** around 2030.
feel: **Uneasy**, but it feels like something for **later**.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that I'd probably just keep my head down and enjoy the football, which I know is exactly what I shouldn't do.
fieldNote: He admits he'd **drift**, which is honest for someone who resists change.
He names a **warning sign**: AI on the non-league coverage.
His **coaching badges** are a real, hands-on fallback he undervalues.

steps.text: Keep reporting until the paper uses AI for non-league coverage
Buy a house with Hana in about two years
Look at coaching work around 2030 using his coaching badges

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have no time and no plan, and I'd be the first name off the desk. What would help is the government paying for proper retraining while you're still working, and a club or paper that gives juniors a chance to move into the hands-on side.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people like me aren't anti-technology. I'm not against the machines, I just don't see why I should be the first one to hand over my notebook.

headlineQuote: I'm not against the machines, I just don't see why I should be the first one to hand over my notebook.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old** sports reporter at a regional evening paper, covering a second-tier football club.
He never uses **AI tools**, prefers being at the ground and keeps his views offline.
Eight months of savings and his fiancée's **pharmacy job** give them room as their wedding nears.
He goes from **uneasy** about paper cuts to alarmed if AGI comes in two years.
With more time, he'd aim for **club media work** or coaching, the hands-on side.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no time, no plan, and be first off the desk.
whatWouldHelp: Employers giving juniors a path into **hands-on roles**.
